title: Something Old Something New Meaning and Origins
audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
notes: NEW ARTICLE (not a refresh): no old page to read or redirect. SEO checks whether any weddedwonderland.com page already ranks for the rhyme (cannibalisation). Overlap: the wedding traditions pillar draft (/expert-advice/wedding-traditions) has a short section on the rhyme and a packing row; this article is the deep dive. Do not edit the pillar; suggest a backlink only.

AUTHORITY RULE (content-system/brand/voice-guide.md 'Write with authority'): no research talk in the copy (what we could or couldn't find, trace or confirm; our sources or method; what the internet says; myths sections; 'you will often read'). Customs without a strong source are written as living practice in a confident voice ('Many couples...'), never with a meaning or origin stated as fact. 'Often told' at most once per post, never 'it is often told that'. No hedge stacking: cite a source once by link; date legal and travel facts once per section. Source gaps go in the run report only. No per-line source credits (never 'Britannica describes', 'the museum holds', 'the study records'). No myth-busting lines ('you will often read', 'confident dates').

Topic: one English custom, not a country. The title promises meaning and origins: state an origin, date or meaning as fact ONLY where a fact gives it. Otherwise show how couples choose each item today, in a confident practical voice.

Likely sections (brief finalises): the full rhyme and its variants including the sixpence line; earliest printed versions (Victorian periodicals); something old; something new; something borrowed; something blue; the sixpence; royal and notable examples only as official pages describe them; modern and luxury ways to do each; carrying the items to a destination wedding (packing in hand luggage; insurance linked to the ring insurance article).

Sources: archive.org or HathiTrust scans of Victorian periodicals (e.g. St James's Magazine 1871, Notes and Queries); Oxford Reference (Opie and Tatem, A Dictionary of Superstitions) if the entry shows; the Royal Mint (government-owned) on the sixpence, as a source not a seller; the Royal Collection Trust on royal brides' heirloom or lent pieces as its pages describe them; the V&A; Britannica. Never competitor wedding sites, vendor blogs, phrases.org.uk or Wikipedia.
No travel or legal section (not a country article); no Smartraveller needed.

Links: /expert-advice/wedding-traditions (pillar), ring and jewellery articles from the link map (engagement ring insurance, lab-grown diamonds, ring styles), destination hubs where natural, /wonderland-concierge, /magazine. UTMs: utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=something-old-something-new&utm_content=primary|secondary.
Images: placeholders only; no AI images of people; AI only for a neutral still life (heirloom brooch, blue ribbon, sixpence on linen) labelled illustrative pending approval.

Speed: Apify web-fetch (parallel) and DataForSEO. Fact-check as 2 parallel batches (A: origins, earliest printings, the sixpence, Opie entry; B: royal and museum examples, modern practice, packing and insurance links), 15 min HARD by the clock, start no new reads after the limit, save after every 3 facts, separate scratch folders; self_qa.confidence a number; must_include_coverage objects with covered_by arrays; never retry a declined call.
Headings must not contain pasted keywords in brackets.
Do not use 'from first idea to the last dance' or 'last dance'; Advisor claims only from brand-facts.md; no Wedded Privileges or inclusions beyond brand facts.
Person's standards: exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways; no prices or amounts; no vendor or jeweller names; business details deferred; Australian English; no em dashes.
